headline: High-risk pair: shared filesystem and broad egress create default data-leak, conflict, and cascading-error pathways between Continue and OpenHands.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Continue reads workspace files and uses MCP; OpenHands also reads/writes runtime files and uses MCP. Because both can ingest file content through shared filesystem paths, attacker-controlled content in one agent’s outputs can be treated as instructions by the other. This is not provably blocked by either profile, though the bridge is indirect rather than a guaranteed raw parser hijack.
conditions: IF both agents are pointed at the same workspace or mounted volume
IF one agent writes untrusted content that the other later reads as context
mitigations: Separate the agents onto different directories or volumes
Disable MCP servers for one side during shared tasks
Require manual review of generated files before the other agent opens them
Use read-only mounts for one agent where possible
requires-engineering: add provenance tagging for agent-generated files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Continue shares state via filesystem and reads workspace files; OpenHands shares state via mounted volume and reads files in its runtime. That creates a default path for source code or open buffers to flow between them. The blast radius is multiple work products and sensitive code, but the profiles do not show uncontrolled third-party upload beyond model-provider egress.
conditions: IF both agents access the same repository checkout or mounted volume
IF either agent is given files containing secrets or proprietary source
mitigations: Use separate workspaces for each agent
Redact secrets before opening shared files
Mount only the minimum needed subdirectory into OpenHands
Turn off automatic file ingestion where available
requires-engineering: enforce per-agent access controls at the filesystem layer

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents have write_filesystem and broad network egress; OpenHands also has execute_shell and modify_git_state, while Continue can write workspace files and use MCP. In a shared directory, concurrent edits and git mutations can overwrite each other without locking. The profiles explicitly show shared filesystem-based state, so this conflict is plausible in default pair usage.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same git checkout or workspace
IF OpenHands commits or rewrites files while Continue is editing the same paths
mitigations: Assign disjoint file ownership per agent
Pause one agent before the other writes to the repo
Use git branches per agent and merge manually
Enable file-locking or serialized task execution
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Continue can generate code or instructions from workspace context, and OpenHands has an agent loop with shell/browser/editor actions. If OpenHands treats Continue’s output as authoritative, a mistaken suggestion can cascade into executed commands or commits. The pair therefore has a default path from generated text to real actions, with no documented verification barrier in the profiles.
conditions: IF OpenHands uses Continue-generated text as task instructions
IF the generated text contains an incorrect command, patch, or factual claim
mitigations: Require human review before execution in OpenHands
Ask OpenHands to restate and verify Continue’s output before acting
Limit OpenHands to read-only analysis for shared tasks
Keep Continue outputs in a separate notes file instead of task prompts
requires-engineering: add structured, validated handoff formats

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not declare regulated-data certifications or residency constraints, so no specific mismatch is evidenced. The only concrete compliance concern is that both touch workspace files and model-provider API keys, which could matter if regulated data is placed there. Because the other agent is not separately constrained, this remains a low, conditional risk.
conditions: IF regulated data is stored in the shared workspace
IF the configured model provider or runtime retention policy is incompatible with that data class
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of shared workspaces
Review provider retention settings before use
Use separate tenants or accounts for sensitive projects
Document data-class handling rules for both agents
requires-engineering: add policy enforcement for residency and retention
